summary:
What we built: Flame in Freefall is a Streamlit dashboard built entirely on NASA’s public (CC0) Physical Sciences Informatics data with 403 real test points from the FLEX and BASS-II microgravity combustion experiments.

How it meets the challenge: The challenge asks us to make sense of how fire behaves in freefall. We turn that raw NASA data into clear, usable fire-safety answers, rank experiments by crew risk, dial in a cabin condition and see whether a fire would catch and spread (with the exact test points behind the verdict), ask fire-safety questions and get cite-only answers, and browse sourced insights. Every result is traceable to real data, with an honest “no data” instead of a guess.

Why it matters: Fire is one of the gravest hazards aboard a spacecraft, and it behaves unlike Earth, burning at lower oxygen, often nearly invisible, slipping past standard detectors. Earth-based testing has a blind spot this makes visible.
details:
What it does
Flame in Freefall is an interactive dashboard that makes NASA’s real microgravity fire-test data usable for crew-safety decisions. It has four tools: an Experiment Atlas that catalogues the NASA experiments we use and ranks each by how dangerous its findings are for a crew; a Risk Envelope where you set a cabin condition (material, oxygen, pressure) and see whether a fire would catch and spread, based on the nearest real test points; an Ask the Corpus Q&A that answers fire-safety questions using only cited NASA material (or refuses when nothing matches); and an Insights Feed of key crew-safety takeaways, each carrying a source link.

How it works
We downloaded NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets — FLEX (droplet combustion) and BASS-II (solid flame spread) — and built a pipeline that cleans the raw CSVs into a unified set of 403 test points (build_dataset.py → JSON files the app reads). The Risk Envelope isn’t a black box: it finds the nearest real test points to your condition, reports what fraction burned, and labels the confidence measured / interpolated / no-data — saying “no data” rather than guessing when nothing comparable was tested. The crew-risk score is a transparent 0–100 (oxygen risk + detection difficulty + material realism). Ask the Corpus uses TF-IDF retrieval over the NASA corpus and returns the top cited passage extractively — it never generates or invents claims.

Benefits
Every answer is traceable to real NASA data, with the evidence shown on screen and DOIs to the source datasets. It turns dense experimental tables into something a crew member, spacecraft designer, or student can actually explore and trust. Because it refuses rather than bluffs, it’s a reference you can rely on.

What we hope to achieve
We want to make the fire-safety lessons buried in NASA’s combustion research visible and usable — helping spacecraft designers choose safer cabin materials, mission planners weigh atmosphere trade-offs, and anyone understand why fire in space is a distinct hazard. Next, we’d wire in more investigations and add partial-gravity (Moon/Mars) data.

Tools, languages, software
Python, with Streamlit (the app), Plotly (charts), pandas (data handling), scikit-learn (TF-IDF retrieval), and pytest (14 unit + integration tests). Built in VS Code with a conda environment, versioned on GitHub. All data is NASA PSI (CC0, public domain). No paid APIs or special hardware — it runs on a standard laptop.

Creativity & factors we considered
Our core design choice was honesty: a tool that shows its sources, admits its limits, and says “no data” instead of fabricating an answer. We deliberately scoped to two well-understood investigations rather than over-claiming breadth, kept the whole pipeline reproducible, and wrote every feature so a non-specialist could follow it.
